brief.situation: 11:00 in a level III NICU. You are the pediatric physical therapist. Baby Torres was born at 27 weeks and is now 31 weeks corrected age, on nasal CPAP, with tight hip and shoulder positioning from lying extended. You planned gentle range of motion and positioning after his care time.
handover: His nurse says he 'had a rough morning' with two self-resolving desaturations during his bath.

Unit developmental care policy: watch for stress cues during handling; pause and contain for stress cues; stop and call the bedside nurse for a heart rate under 100 or saturation under 85% that does not recover quickly.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What are Baby Torres's cues telling you, and what do you change?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Finger splay, arching, hiccups, mottling and a falling heart rate and saturation are stress and disorganization cues; a 31-week infant on CPAP cannot tolerate this handling now.
parts.modelAnswer: He's stressed: fingers splayed, arching, hiccups, mottled, and his heart rate and sats are dropping. He can't handle this right now.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Pauses, contains him in flexion with hands to face, quiets the area, watches him recover, tells his nurse and changes to short, cue-based sessions with positioning.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop, tuck him into flexion with his hands to his face, quiet everything, let him recover, tell his nurse, and switch to short sessions that follow his cues.

scoring.modelReasoning: In the NICU, preterm infants show stress and disorganization through color changes, vital sign changes, gaze aversion, finger splaying, hiccups, yawning and limb extension. Slow down or give the infant a break when stress signs appear, use supports to keep the infant flexed, and resume gradually as he stabilizes. Physical therapy in the NICU is cue-based: baseline first, short sessions at care times, positioning that supports flexion, and communication with the bedside nurse.
